articles.title: How Canada could hit back to hurt the US economy - and Trump
articles.summary: What leverage does Canada, which sells about 70% of its exports to the US, actually have in this spiralling trade dispute?
articles.body:
About 70% of Canada's exported goods go to the US. So what leverage does it have in this spiralling trade dispute with its southern neighbour, which also happens to be the world's largest economy?

Canada is the top customer for 26 US states, including Maine, Michigan, and Wisconsin. And it is in the top three for 45 of the 50 American states, suggesting Prime Minister Mark Carney has room to manoeuvre in a trade fight.

For now, Carney's planned Canadian retaliatory duties are strategic "dollar-for-dollar" countermeasures focused on steel, dairy, appliances, agricultural equipment, electronics, pulp and paper - though the list is still being finalised.

Polls suggest a majority of Canadians would be unhappy if his government went in the other direction and made significant concessions to the US. That sentiment is shared by Ontario Premier Doug Ford, one of Trump's most vocal critics north of the border, who responded to the tariff threats by telling the US president to "kiss my ass".

Canada's Finance Department said additional measures to protect workers and businesses would be announced on Tuesday.

Here are some areas where Canada can apply economic pressure.

Carney noted on Saturday that Canada supplies the vast majority of US natural gas and electricity imports and about 60% of crude oil imports.

"I don't think they want us to stop sending any of that energy," he said.

Squeezing the US on energy is not in the current countermeasures, although various political officials have said explicitly it wasn't ruled out - and not all provincial premiers have been keen to use that leverage.

Ford, whose Ontario province is home to Canada's auto manufacturing industry, is open to how far the dispute could go and said that an "energy surcharge is on the table".

He briefly floated a 25% surcharge in 2025 on all electricity exports to the United States, which his government estimated would have impacted 1.5 million homes and businesses in Michigan, Minnesota and New York.

The country is also a major source of important commodities including potash - a product in fertiliser for which Canada is the world's top supplier.

"I'd love to see [Trump] run cars without any oil. I'll love to see him grow vegetables and fruit without the potash," Ford said on Monday. "President Trump underestimates us, and that's the biggest mistake."

Canada announces 'dollar-for-dollar' retaliatory tariffs on US as high as 50% Published 4 hours ago

Canada announces 'dollar-for-dollar' retaliatory tariffs on US as high as 50%

Canada also has significant reserves of critical minerals like lithium, nickel and graphite.

The US is Canada's top destination for overall mineral exports, another point where Ottawa could apply pressure.

Ford here also took the lead, saying in an interview with the Associated Press that the US "won't get a grain of sand out of Ontario".

Canada has already proven that it can cause economic pain in the US.

Even before trade talks broke down, a decision by most provinces to ban US alcohol from liquor store shelves - in response to the first wave of US tariffs early last year - dealt a devastating blow to that industry in the US.

American wine had a significant collapse in exports, one the Wine Institute called the "most significant market disruption in decades".

US wine exports to Canada fell 78% year over year, a $357m (C$494m; £261m) loss in export value, according to government data. The distillers association reported similar numbers - saying provincial bans have caused exports of American spirits to drop by more than 70%.

That boycott remains in place in 11 of the 13 Canadian provinces and territories. The ban is a point of significant frustration for the Trump administration.

While that alcohol boycott has been put in place by political leaders, there are also grassroots decisions by many Canadians that have hurt their neighbour's economy - such as avoiding travel to the US.

Even with a slight uptick in road trips to the US in April, Canadians made 800,000 fewer trips that month compared to the same time in 2024, before Trump returned to office, according to national data.

The travel boycott has meant a loss of about C$3.3bn ($2.35bn; £1.75bn) in revenue for the US last year. Some American cities and states have appealed for Canadians to return through targeted advertisements and special deals.

Timing and Canadian political will could also be a tool for negotiations.

Canadians know they will feel economic pain in this dispute - financial analysts estimated the most recent tariffs of 50% on about $20bn of Canadian imports could trim between 0.3% to 0.6% off the country's GDP in the short term.

Still, a majority in the country broadly back Ottawa's decision to drive a hard bargain against the Trump administration, and other Canadian political leaders have shown a united front.

A weekend poll from Angus Reid indicated that some 76% of Canadians support Ottawa's decision to walk away from trade negotiations even as they worry for their own job security.

The US midterm elections are fast approaching, with the economy front and centre for voters and the Republican hold on Congress looking tenuous.

Two of the biggest Senate races are in Michigan and Maine, which both border Canada and send most of their exports there.

The Yale Budget Lab calculates that under current law, Trump's global tariffs will cost American households about $1,100 annually.

Any further increase in the costs of goods and the wider impact of the trade dispute on businesses could further sour the American public on the economy.

On Monday, Carney said that US workers will be hurt by Trump's most recent threat to increase tariff on autos and auto parts from Canada to 50% after 1 January.

"What is the message sent out to the workers in Michigan, Ohio, Kentucky, Alabama? These workers depend absolutely on Canada, their largest consumer," he said, adding that Canada buys more American cars than the EU and other countries.

On CNN on Monday, British Columbia Premier David Eby noted US consumers will see the impact of the US tariffs in any number of goods.

"If you're building a new home, on plywood, if you're replacing your floor, on veneers, if you're getting married, on cut flowers, if you're going out fishing, on fishing poles," he said.

"It is a bizarre policy for Americans. It's going to hurt them."

Ford, one of the most vocal Canadian leaders opposing the Trump administration's tariffs, also did not rule out specifically targeting Republican US states with retaliatory measures and "making sure America's economy feels the pain".

As for the coming midterms, Ford said: "If I were allowed to, I'd be down there door-knocking".

articles.title: In 2025, Mowi launched Chileâs first floating solar salmon farm; now it supplies 57% of its power and saving 36,750 gallons of diesel a year

articles.body: For years, diesel has been a practical part of running salmon farms in remote coastal waters, where connecting to a conventional electricity grid is often difficult. That is beginning to change at one of Mowiâs sites in southern Chile. In June 2025, the company introduced what it described as Chileâs first floating solar cage at its Isla Huar salmon farm in the Los Lagos region. The installation combines solar panels fitted to the farming structure with batteries that can store electricity for use when sunlight is unavailable. A year on, the project is reported to be supplying about 57% of the siteâs power requirements. It is also expected to save around 139,200 litres of diesel each year, equivalent to roughly 36,750 US gallons. The figures offer an early indication of what renewable power can do for an offshore salmon farm operating far from the grid.Why Mowiâs 2025 floating solar cage in Chile mattersMowi announced the project in June 2025, describing it as Chileâs first floating solar cage. The installation was developed with AKVA group, Alotta Energy and Fjord Maritime at the companyâs Isla Huar operation. Rather than placing solar panels on land, the system puts them directly on the floating farming infrastructure, where they have to cope with wind, waves and the demands of an offshore working environment.According to the official Mowi site, the hybrid arrangement was designed to reduce fuel use and cut emissions. The company estimated an annual reduction of 350 tonnes of COâ. Its announcement also explained how the electricity would be handled: power from the floating solar plant could either be used immediately or stored in batteries for later use. The system was initially expected to cover up to half of the centreâs energy requirements.How battery storage keeps Mowiâs floating solar salmon farm runningThe panels are only part of the system. Battery storage is what allows electricity generated during periods of sunshine to remain available when solar production falls. Alotta, which supplied the floating solar technology, describes the installation as a hybrid system designed to provide power continuously rather than simply producing electricity when the sun is shining.In its account of the Chilean project, Alotta said the system covers approximately 50% of the siteâs energy requirements and combines solar generation with integrated battery storage. The company also operates the project under an energy-as-a-service model, meaning Mowi purchases renewable electricity rather than having to operate the entire energy installation itself. Alotta described the arrangement as a way of making the technology easier to use at remote aquaculture sites.Why cutting diesel use matters for Mowiâs remote salmon farmThe newer figures from AKVA group put the renewable contribution at around 57% of the farmâs energy needs. The company says the system is expected to reduce annual diesel consumption by approximately 139,200 litres. That is roughly 36,750 US gallons of fuel that would no longer need to be burned each year. The same reduction is associated with about 350 tonnes of COâ emissions annually.That reduction matters at a farm that operates away from a conventional electricity grid. Diesel is not only used as a fuel source; it also has to be transported to the site. Cutting consumption therefore reduces the amount of fuel that has to be delivered by boat. AKVA says the project is also expected to reduce noise from diesel generators, changing the working conditions around the farm while lowering the amount of boat traffic associated with refuelling.Why Mowiâs floating solar project could become a model for remote salmon farmsThe project is attracting attention because remote aquaculture sites often need reliable electricity but are located far from conventional power grids. Solar panels and battery storage can provide local power, while diesel generators remain available when renewable energy is insufficient. As per Alotta, its floating solar technology was previously tested along the Norwegian coast before being introduced in Chile. Mowi developed the project with AKVA group, Alotta Energy and Fjord Maritime to improve energy efficiency and reduce emissions.For Mowi, the goal is to reduce diesel use rather than eliminate it. The reported 57% renewable contribution means solar power and batteries supply a significant share of the farmâs electricity, with diesel kept as backup. If the projected 139,200-litre annual reduction is achieved, the system could also reduce the amount of fuel that needs to be transported to the remote site.Launched in 2025 as Chileâs first floating solar-powered salmon-farming installation, the project demonstrates how renewable energy and battery storage can be added to existing offshore operations. The technology partners say the system is designed to provide about 57% of the farmâs electricity and cut diesel use by roughly 36,750 gallons a year, potentially offering a model for other remote aquaculture sites.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Wife of active-duty Army sergeant deported amid Trump's immigration campaign
articles.summary: An advocacy group says some military families are now "living in the shadows."
articles.body:
The wife of an Army sergeant and mother of a 6-year-old was deported on Monday.

Army Sgt. Hedar Leonel Turcios Juarez confirmed that his wife, Cristy Maryori Villafranca Trejo, was deported to Honduras. Turcios's wife's deportation comes as Trump's immigration crackdown impacts active-duty military spouses.

Turcios Juarez previously told ABC News that ICE officers detained Villafranca outside a Walmart in July as the couple's young daughter watched. Villafranca left Honduras in 2016 due to violent crime in the country, her husband said.

After attending high school in the U.S., he joined the military and became a U.S. citizen in 2024 after a nine-month deployment to the Middle East. Then he began pursuing citizenship for his wife, hoping his service would help expedite her naturalization process, he said.

"She's been a very supportive wife since the first day that I decided to join the military. I was deployed for nine months. She took care of my family," Turcios said of his spouse when she was detained. "She's not a threat to anybody. We're just trying to keep our family together."

The Department of Homeland Security confirmed the removal of Cristy Maryori Villafranca-Trejo, the wife of an army sergeant.

"On August 24, Cristy Maryori Villafranca-Trejo, an illegal alien from Honduras, was removed from the United States in accordance with our laws," a spokesperson for DHS said in a statement.

"On July 11, ICE conducted a targeted immigration enforcement operation to arrest Cristy Maryori Villafranca-Trejo, an illegal alien from Honduras," the spokesperson added. "Villafranca-Trejo illegally entered the United States in 2016 and was released into the country under the Obama administration."

Judge strikes down Trump administration policy that suspended immigrant visas for 75 countries, reinstating evaluations

Turcios' family is hardly alone. President Donald Trump's mass deportation campaign has swept up more than 50 parents and spouses of service members during his second term, with at least six deported, according to an investigation by the Associated Press.

Danitza James, CEO of Repatriate Our Patriots, which works with Families United to help active-duty service members and veterans reunite their families, said that, beyond providing legal representation, the organization's only other strategy has been to call Congress to request help.

She said she is currently working with eight active-duty service members and one veteran whose family members have been detained as of Aug. 20. ABC News spoke with two of the families that she is working to unite.

Trump admin sends 1st deportation flight to Haiti since ending temporary protected status

The cases complicate one of the administration's central arguments for its aggressive expansion of immigration enforcement. Trump has repeatedly said ICE is targeting the "worst of the worst," and has described immigrants who entered the U.S. illegally as "animals" and "dangerous criminals" that should not be in the country.

An ABC News review of state and federal records did not find criminal records for any of the military spouses named in this story in the states where they live.

"She's been a very supportive wife since the first day that I decided to join the military. I was deployed for nine months. She took care of my family," Turcios said of his spouse. "She's not a threat to anybody. We're just trying to keep our family together."

Pregnant woman has been held for weeks following immigration lawyer scam, family says

The Trump administration's detention of undocumented spouses and parents of active-duty service members comes as the U.S. is at war with Iran, leaving troops without the support of their families and shifting their focus away from their military careers, advocacy groups say. Some have been forced to take leave from duty to care for their children in their spouses' absence, according to advocacy groups and families ABC News interviewed.

"There are so many military families of active-duty service members that are living in the shadows of this immigration machine, that is putting them in fear of seeking resources and asking for help, while their service member is actively serving our country, and sacrificing for our nation," said James of Repatriate Our Patriots.

Military service has long been a pathway to citizenship

For decades, military families have occupied a protected corner of the immigration system, according to the National Military Family Association. Under policies embraced by Republican and Democratic administrations, the undocumented parents and spouses of service members have generally been shielded from deportation.

Military recruiters have also long promoted military service as a pathway to citizenship, including through programs which can allow undocumented relatives of troops to remain in the country while applying for a green card and work authorization.

The bargain extends to troops themselves. Green card holders can join the U.S. military and troops can apply for naturalization after a year of honorable service, an incentive that stretches back to the Civil War. During World War I, Congress went further, streamlining the citizenship process for troops whose enlistment could effectively mean automatic citizenship.

Virginia woman says ICE agent pointed gun at her, denies trying to run over agents

"Having a family member in the military is not a free pass to violate our nation's laws," a DHS spokesperson said in response to the recent arrest by ICE of the father of an active-duty sailor for alleged immigration violations. "Military service by an immediate relative does not automatically grant parole, lawful status, or immunity from immigration enforcement."

Racial and ethnic minorities are making up a growing share of the military. In the Army, the Pentagon's largest service by far, Hispanic recruits grew from about 19% of new enlistees in 2020 to nearly 27% last year, according to internal service data reviewed by ABC News.

Naturalizations through military service have also more than tripled over roughly the same period, rising from about 4,500 in 2020 to 16,000 in 2024, according to Department of Homeland Security data. The Philippines, Mexico, Jamaica and Nigeria were among the leading countries of origin for troops who became U.S. citizens through their service.

Turcios left Honduras in 2014, also to escape violence in the country, he said. After attending high school in the U.S. he joined the military and became a U.S. citizen in 2024 after a nine-month deployment to the Middle East. Then he began pursuing citizenship for his wife, hoping his service would help expedite her naturalization process, he said.

ACLU sues DHS over 'inhumane conditions' at nation's largest immigration detention facility

Instead, Villafranca, undocumented spouses and parents of many other active-duty military personnel have been forced into detention, according to lawyers, advocacy groups and military families.

Villafranca relayed allegedly inhumane conditions in Camp East Montana, according to her husband. The facility is the country's largest detention center, which sits on land formerly used for Japanese-American internment camps during World War II.

Turcios said his wife had to wear the same clothes for about four days. Access to clean clothing remained an issue until he reached out to Rep. Veronica Escobar, D- Texas, who sent an inquiry to ICE regarding Villafranca's lack of clean clothing. Turcios said that after a few weeks, they finally fixed the issue.

​Army Staff Sgt. Alexis Jaramillo has served in the military for 11 years and is currently stationed at Fort Polk, Louisiana. His wife, Maisa Lopes Eliaser, came to the U.S. from São Paulo, Brazil, in 2019 on a tourist visa, which she had overstayed while Jaramillo was helping her pursue citizenship.

She was taken into custody in front of Jaramillo, who was dressed in uniform, and their five-year-old son during an appointment to be interviewed to get her green card.

Lopes Eliaser spent two days in Pickens County Jail in Georgia before being transferred to the South Louisiana ICE Processing Center, where she slept in a large room with approximately 80 people for about six weeks, her husband said.

​On July 13, Lopes Eliaser said ICE officers put her on a bus to the Alexandria International Airport in Louisiana. She was then flown to Bogotá, Colombia, where the plane stopped before its final destination, Brazil. During the layover, Lopes Eliaser called her husband using someone else's phone, he said.

Jaramillo said he had been communicating with Sen. Mark Kelly, a Navy veteran, about his wife's case before she was taken to the airport. When Lopes Eliaser disappeared from the detainee-tracking app that Jaramillo was checking, he contacted Kelly again to ask for help bringing her home.

"Maisa's case is an example of this administration's focus on targeting the loved ones of those who've stepped up to serve our country. It's wrong and makes no sense at all," Kelly wrote in a statement to ABC News.

Kelly's office told ABC News that his casework team established communications with the ICE field office and kept Jaramillo updated.

DHS did not respond to a request for comment on Eliaser's case at the time.

Jaramillo credits Kelly for contacting ICE and getting Lopes Eliaser eventually returned to the U.S. When she landed in Brazil, she was flown back to the Alexandria International Airport without ever stepping off the airplane. Jaramillo and Lopes Eliaser were reunited and are currently together at their home in Louisiana.

Padres minor league coach detained by ICE at El Paso airport

​"That was a nightmare. That was a really, really nightmare," Jaramillo said. "I'm never going to explain best how difficult it was and still is."

​While Jaramillo and Lopes Eliaser are now united, they are still dealing with the aftermath of her detention and deportation. Jaramillo had to take leave to care for his son and fight to get his wife back. Now that his wife is back home, he said he will return to service on Monday.

Since Lopes Eliaser was first detained, Jaramillo said he has incurred more than $7,000 in legal fees and costs associated with submitting paperwork, approximately equal to over a month's pay.

​Jaramillo said his wife is still experiencing health issues from the conditions of detention, which he said were crowded and where she also lacked access to clean clothing. Jarmillo said he took her to see a doctor Thursday.

Petition filed days before ICE detainee's death cited medical conditions while seeking his release

​James said that many of the other cases of active-duty military service members' families being detained have involved members of Congress making calls to reunite families.

Kelly has publicly been involved with two other cases of military families targeted by the Trump administration for deportation.

​In a letter sent Aug. 9 to DHS, the Defense Department and the Department of Veterans Affairs, congressional Democrats wrote that they will investigate whether the Pentagon and DHS are coordinating to deport military service members and their families.

​"The best way to bring change to this is to the legislative or policy, because this should not be a phone call. This should not be a one-case change," James said. "This is clearly impacting more than 50 military spouses and cases across the board, and there needs to be a change that is codified."

articles.title: France tornado: Village of Pomas ravaged and dozens hurt
articles.summary: The south-western village of Pomas was hardest hit, with hundreds of homes damaged and fifteen people taken to hospital.
articles.body:
A tornado has torn through the village of Pomas in south-west France, injuring 39 people and damaging hundreds of homes.

Authorities said 15 people were taken to hospital and two were in a critical condition. One man said his pregnant wife was injured after their house collapsed on her.

More than 120 emergency workers were deployed to the village south of Carcassonne after winds reaching 117km/h (73mph) tore roofs off houses and damaged an estimated 300 homes on Monday.

"Half the village has been destroyed," said one resident called Pierre, who described the tornado as swirling like a "huge red and yellow chimney".

"There's a huge castle and a third of it is has collapsed - even though these are stones that have stood for 1,000 years," Pierre told Ici Occitanie.

The third stage of the Vuelta a España cycle race, which was taking place in the Aude area of south-western France, had to be cancelled when a hail storm forced the riders to take shelter about 15km from the finish line.

The extreme weather has left about 2,800 homes across 10 villages without electricity, according to officials.

Local sub-prefect Emmanuelle Plantier-Lemarchand told French radio that she was not aware of anyone missing. She lowered the number of victims from 41 to 39, and said 15 of them had been treated in hospital.

"I heard this massive noise... then I saw everything flying around in the air and my roof collapsed over my head," shocked resident Chantal told French radio. "I've got no house left, that's for sure... I was really scared. I thought that's it, this my final hour."

French authorities had issued an orange alert for thunderstorms in large parts of the country's south-west, which have already been hit by power outages and transport disruptions.

Eyewitness footage from the region captured the swirling vortex of the tornado looming in the horizon above houses and trees.

Images from the small village of Pomas, which was the hardest hit, showed uprooted trees, damaged cars and rubble from destroyed homes.

Meanwhile there were flight delays and cancellations at airports in Bordeaux, Marseille, Nice, Toulouse and north of Paris to the north, said Transport Minister Philippe Tabarot.

On average, France experiences several dozen tornadoes per year, according to the country's national weather service Météo-France.

It comes after Europe's summer of unprecedented heatwaves and wildfires, with France's south-west region among the worst affected with an area of 42,000 hectares burnt in one of the largest forest fires since World War Two.

would complicate diplomatic efforts.Pezeshkian made the remarks during a meeting with Munir in Tehran on Monday, according to the official website of the Iranian President.Munir arrived in Iran for talks with Iranian officials amid heightened regional tensions and continuing friction between Tehran and Washington.The Iranian president also expressed hope that continued cooperation between Iran and Pakistan would help achieve the goals outlined in a 14-point Memorandum of Understanding (MoU).âThe United States must correct its tone and approach in its interactions with Iran, because relying on coercion and bullying will only complicate the implementation processes,â Pezeshkian said.He stressed that Washington should adhere to its commitments to Iran based on international law and standards.Pezeshkian also said Iran would withstand pressure by relying on national solidarity.âOur nation will overcome any pressure and threat by relying on this solidarity,â he said.Pezeshkian stresses regional cooperation, unityDuring the meeting, Pezeshkian stressed the need for lasting peace and security in the region and called for greater cooperation with Islamic countries and neighbouring states.âThe Islamic Republic of Iran is ready for any cooperation and interaction in the economic, political, and security dimensions with Islamic countries and neighbours, because the Holy Prophet (PBUH) has always commanded peace and friendship,â he said.He also emphasised the importance of unity among Islamic countries, describing it as a deterrent against what he called the âconspiracies of the Zionist regime and the enemies of Islamâ.âThe unity and cohesion of Islamic countries is the most important deterrent against the conspiracies of the Zionist regime and the enemies of Islam, and if this convergence is realised, the enemies will not be able to advance their sinister goals,â Pezeshkian said.The Iranian president also referred to coordination within Iran to advance regional peace and stability and expressed hope that Pakistan's diplomatic efforts would contribute to stability in the region.He said he hoped the âIslamic world will achieve increasing growth, dignity, and prideâ.Munir, in turn, thanked Pezeshkian for his efforts towards establishing regional stability and peace.âIn order to advance common goals and achieve a comprehensive agreement, it is essential that diplomatic processes be discussed and examined with complete precision and meticulousness,â Munir said, according to the Iranian president's official website.The Pakistan Army chief also welcomed the growing trend of bilateral cooperation between the two countries.He said the âdeep historical, religious and cultural commonalities between Pakistan and Iran are a valuable asset for overcoming the current complex circumstances and charting a bright futureâ.Munirâs Iran visit follows Trump callMunir's visit to Tehran comes after he "ICE lodged a detainer on August 20 for Isaac Melendez-Carranza, an illegal alien from El Salvador, with the Loudoun County Jail," a DHS spokesperson told Fox News. U.S. Border Patrol arrested Melendez-Carranza near Hebbronville, Texas, on May 3, 2016, after he illegally entered the U.S. via the Rio Grande, according to DHS. articles.title: French tourist dies in Death Valley after car gets stuck in mud
articles.summary: The 68-year-old man was found dead in California's salt flats amid 116°F (46.6C) heat.
articles.body:
A French tourist has died in California's Death Valley after becoming stranded on the side of the road during 46.6C (116F) heat.

Police found 68-year-old Pierre Michel Formosa recently following a brief search, with the National Park service saying he died while trying to seek help in the blistering heat when his car got stuck in mud.

"This is a heartbreaking reminder of how quickly conditions here can turn dangerous," Death Valley National Park Superintendent Mike Reynolds said in a statement.

Soaring temperatures across the United States have caused millions of people to sweat through record heatwaves, leading to dozens of heat-related deaths.

Formosa was driving through Death Valley with his French travelling companion last Monday when their vehicle became stuck in mud on West Side Road.

The pair sought help by walking across the salt flats, before severe heat prevented the 68-year-old from continuing after 1.3 miles, according to the Death Valley National Park.

The travelling companion managed to hail down a nearby driver, before rangers and police found Formosa later that afternoon where he was pronounced dead.

"Death Valley is an extraordinary place, but its heat, distances, and remoteness can be dangerous, regardless of experience," Reynolds said.

"We're grateful to everyone who took part in the search, and our thoughts are with his loved ones."

Coroners would determine the cause and manner of his death, the national park said.

An extreme heat warning is currently in effect across Death Valley, which brands itself as the "hottest place on Earth", according to its official website, having recorded a global high of 57C (134F) in 1913.

Forecasters at the National Weather Service expected Southern California would experience its "hottest week of summer so far", the bureau said in a recent statement.

Record heatwaves have endangered tourists visiting US landmarks throughout the summer.

At least four hikers died in June while trekking through the Grand Canyon , state authorities reported in Arizona.

articles.title: Target Pulls Clown Halloween Costume After Backlash, Says ‘We Got This Wrong’ in Apology Note
articles.summary: The costume was called out on social media for being racially insensitive
articles.body:
Target has removed a Halloween costume after it was criticized for resembling blackface and racist minstrel show imagery. The retail franchise also issued an apology on Monday, Aug. 24

The costume featured a Black child model in a pose linked to Jim Crow-era stereotypes, sparking widespread backlash

The controversy follows Target's rollback of DEI initiatives and ongoing criticism from consumers and company stakeholders

Target has removed a clown Halloween costume following criticisms that it evoked blackface, minstrel shows and racist imagery.

"An apology from us: We removed an offensive Halloween costume that should never have been part of our assortment," Target wrote in a statement shared on social media on Monday, Aug. 24. "It is no longer for sale. As a company, we got this wrong, and we are deeply sorry."

"We know this is especially hurtful for our Black guests, team members and partners," the statement from Target continued. "Removing the costume is an important first step, and we are looking closely at how this happened and what needs to change to ensure this won't happen again."

In photos of the now-deleted costume, sold as "Kids' Glows under Blacklight Circus Clown," a young Black boy modeled the outfit, which featured a black-and-orange printed bodysuit and hood with an exaggerated smile and mini top hat.

The model's pose, in which he stands with one leg and arm raised in a waving gesture, particularly sparked criticism for its affiliation with Jim Crow-era negative depictions of Black people, according to The Cut.

"Target, for real? I'm not surprised, but this is a new low," comedian LaTrez Anderson said in a now-deleted Instagram Reel about the costume, per the outlet.

"The amount of people this costume had to go through to get approved says A. LOT. WHAT YEAR IS IT!?" an Instagram user commented on Target's apology post.

Blackface is defined as "dark makeup worn to mimic the appearance of a Black person and especially to mock or ridicule Black people," according to Merriam-Webster . The use of blackface in the U.S. was initially recorded through "minstrel shows," in which white performers would wear blackface and mock Black people based on negative stereotypes, according to the National Museum of African American History and Culture .

The Halloween costume controversy comes nearly a year after Target rolled back Diversity, Equity, and Inclusion (DEI) initiatives. Target CEO Brian Cornell later stepped down after 11 years with the company, it announced in August 2025. Target has faced consumer boycotts since early last year due to the DEI cuts, PEOPLE previously reported.

Anne and Lucy Dayton, the daughters of one of Target's co-founders, called the company's actions "a betrayal" at the time, CNN previously reported.

articles.title: UK drone factories may face attacks from 'unknown sources', says former Russian minister
articles.summary: The comments on BBC Newsnight come after the UK announced it has agreed to hand over blueprints for British-made missile components to Ukraine.
articles.body:
A Russian former deputy foreign minister has said there might be a "semi-military" response against UK drone factories by "unknown sources" over the sharing of blueprints for British-made cruise missile components .

Andrei Fedorov's comments on BBC Newsnight come as UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham announced plans to travel to the US next month with European leaders to lobby President Donald Trump on Ukraine's defence needs.

Burnham's trip, should it go ahead, would be his first to the US since becoming prime minister.

"Leaving today, I'm quite clear what I need to do in the next few weeks," he said following his visit to Ukraine on Monday, during which he promised to continue pressuring Russia.

The UK has agreed to hand over blueprints for British-made components for the Scalp missile , a French version of the UK's Storm Shadow cruise missile. The blueprints will allow Ukraine to produce the long-range weapon domestically.

Fedorov, a pro-Kremlin commentator who frequently appears on Russian television, said Putin was facing "serious" pressure "to undertake certain measures against UK". Asked on BBC Newsnight where the pressure was coming from, Fedorov responded "public opinion polls, it's coming from journalists, from mass media".

Asked what a "semi-military" response might look like, Fedorov said: "It could take the form of something might happen with enterprises, with factories which are producing drones for Ukraine.

"They could be attacked not by Russia, but by from unknown sources."

The comments are in line with those made by Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov on Monday, when he criticised the UK's decision to share the missile blueprints. Peskov said it prevented "even the slightest progress" towards achieving peace.

He told reporters on Monday that the Russian military was already gathering data to locate any missile production sites to destroy them.

"Britain is involved in this war on the side of the Kyiv regime. Britain methodically and regularly adds fuel to the fire," he added.

In response, Burnham said: "Who started the fire? That's the question, isn't it?"

Burnham's visit to Ukraine was his first official international trip. He met Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky in Kyiv and chaired his first meeting of the "coalition of the willing", set up by the UK and France under his predecessor Sir Keir Starmer.

Burnham has been reaffirming the UK's support for Ukraine in the wake of escalating Russian strikes in recent weeks - including one last week on a shopping centre that killed at least 16 people.

Ukraine has been relying on American supplies of the Patriot interceptor missiles, which are used to combat Russia's ballistic missiles , but stockpiles are running low due to the war in Iran, leaving Ukraine vulnerable to Russian attacks.

Zelensky has said he is hoping to secure 300 patriot missiles ahead of winter, when Russia is likely to increase its attacks on energy infrastructure, as it has done in past years.

In the interview with Bloomberg, Burnham said he felt "really confident" that the issue was "fixable". But he pointed out that it wasn't only the US who could supply Ukraine with Patriots.

"There are other players who could help in the mix who we have influence with," he said. "It's probably going to be a solution that involves a lot of layers and a lot of negotiation."

In July this year, three weeks after offering Ukraine the right to produce Patriots itself, Trump backtracked, saying : "We have not agreed to that. We're talking about it. But it's a hard thing to give away, that kind of technology."

"These weapons are incredible. We have to be very careful about letting somebody build them," Trump told a cabinet meeting.

In a joint statement after the meeting in Ukraine, Burnham and co-chairs French President Emmanuel Macron and German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said the group would aim to strength Kyiv's air defences "as a matter or urgent priority".

They also condemned Moscow's "systemic and escalating strikes against Ukraine's cities, critical infrastructure and civilians" and pledged to "constrain Russia's war chest through sanctions and actions against the shadow fleet".

In a statement ahead of the visit, Burnham said: "On Ukraine's 35th anniversary of independence, the Ukrainian people should be in no doubt: the UK is behind you today and for as long as it takes.

"I am proud of the contribution our country has made to Ukraine and I want the Ukrainian people to hear it directly from me that our support will not waver. After all, Ukraine's security is our security."

He said the friendship Ukraine shared with the UK would "long outlast Russia's illegal war", adding: "Russia should be in no doubt of our resolve. We will not back down until there is a just and lasting peace."

articles.title: Why you should wrap a half-cut lemon in aluminium foil: 5 benefits and other easy storage methods
articles.summary: A lemon rarely gets used all at once. One half may find its way into a cup of tea, a salad, or a recipe. The other often ends up in the refrigerator. .
articles.body: A lemon rarely gets used all at once. One half may find its way into a cup of tea, a salad, or a recipe. The other often ends up in the refrigerator. That half lemon can soon lose its freshness if left uncovered. The cut surface dries out, and its bright citrus aroma fades with time. It may also pick up the smell of nearby food items stored nearby. A simple kitchen habit can help keep that half lemon fresh. Wrap the unused half in aluminium foil and place it in the refrigerator.The foil covers the exposed flesh and creates a barrier against air and surrounding odours. It can also help slow moisture loss and keep the cut surface in better condition. This does not mean a wrapped lemon will stay fresh indefinitely. Cut fruit still needs to be refrigerated and used within a suitable time period. But for a lemon, proper covering can make a noticeable difference.5 reasons to wrap the cut side of a lemon in aluminium foilThe cut side is the part that needs protection. Once the lemon is opened, its flesh meets the air inside the refrigerator, which can cause it to lose its freshness and aroma. Wrapping it gives that exposed surface a simple shield.1. Prevents odour transfer inside the fridgeA half lemon can absorb smells from foods stored around it. Onions, garlic and leftovers can all leave strong aromas in a refrigerator. Aluminium foil covers the exposed flesh and reduces its contact with those smells. This helps the lemon to keep its clean citrus aroma.2. Helps slow moisture lossThe exposed flesh gradually loses moisture when left uncovered. The surface can become dry and shrivelled. A layer of foil helps reduce direct exposure to the dry air moving through the refrigerator. That gives the lemon a better chance of staying juicy until it is used again.3. Helps protect vitamin C and antioxidants from air exposureCutting a lemon exposes its flesh to oxygen. That can contribute to oxidation over time. Covering the cut side limits some of that exposure. It may help slow the loss of vitamin C and other antioxidant compounds. It cannot stop nutrient changes altogether. Fresh lemons are still best to be used without unnecessary delay.4. Keeps the cut surface from becoming tough and leatheryAn uncovered lemon can develop a firm skin across its exposed flesh. It may look dull and feel dry when you finally reach for it. Foil helps protect that surface from the cold circulating air in the fridge. So a cut half is more pleasant to squeeze and use.5. Helps retain its natural citrus aromaThe fresh smell of a lemon is part of what makes it useful in drinks and food. Once cut, the fruit can also absorb competing smells from the fridge. Keeping the cut side covered helps protect its natural citrus character until the next use.What are other ways to preserve a half-cut lemonAluminium foil is quick and convenient. It is not the only choice. A few simple storage methods can protect a leftover lemon while also making better use of reusable kitchen items.Place it in a specialised citrus storage containerA specialised citrus storage container is made to hold cut lemons and other citrus fruits. It covers the exposed end and keeps the fruit contained in the refrigerator. Some designs also hold the lemon firmly so it does not roll around. For people who regularly use half a lemon at a time, it can be a practical reusable option.Store it in an airtight food containerPlace the lemon in an airtight food container with the cut side facing down. Then close the lid firmly. The container reduces exposure to air and helps shield the lemon from strong refrigerator smells.Use a reusable silicone food coverSilicone food covers can fit over the cut end of a lemon. They create a snug barrier without relying on disposable wrapping. They can also be washed and reused. This makes them useful for households that regularly save leftover citrus. The covered lemon should still be kept in the refrigerator.Store the lemon cut-side downPlace the lemon cut-side down in a clean container. This reduces the amount of exposed flesh that comes into contact with air. It works best for short-term storage when the lemon will be used soon. Refrigeration remains important for keeping the cut fruit in good condition.Looking for trusted parenting advice? articles.title: Kaixiao Liu: New Zealand religious sect leader jailed over death of elderly Chinese follower
articles.summary: The body of 70-year-old Shulai Wang was found near a marina in Auckland in 2024.
articles.body:
A New Zealand court has jailed a religious sect leader over the death of an elderly follower who had travelled from China to live with his family.

Kaixiao Liu was found guilty of manslaughter and kidnapping, and sentenced to more than 10 years in prison.

The body of 70-year-old Shulai Wang had been found wrapped in rice bags near Auckland's Gulf Harbour in March 2024, sparking a major homicide investigation which eventually led to Liu.

Liu, a musician who previously appeared in a talent show in China, had denied the charges. He also denied he is a cult leader and said he only attracted followers through his music.

During the trial the court heard that Wang had travelled from Hainan island in China to New Zealand in August 2023.

She moved in with Liu and his family at their house, which Liu had called "the Ark", along with several other female followers.

Prosecutors said that the women acted in "servitude" to Liu and his family, and their lives were tightly controlled by Liu, where they referred to him as "Lord" or "Master".

Wang reportedly spent her days taking care of Liu's children, studying scripture, and planting vegetables.

The court heard that Wang had struggled to comply with the strict rules, possibly due to her old age, and was frequently disciplined.

In March 2024, Wang tried to escape but was caught and restrained. She died later that day, the court heard.

The court heard that Liu, his family, and his followers dumped Wang's body near a marina at Gulf Harbour. Liu had taken his children along for the trip "as camouflage".

The body was found by a fisherman days later. Police eventually traced the rice bags used to wrap Wang's body to Liu, who had made unusually large purchases of that brand of rice.

Besides Liu, his wife, Lanyue Xiao, was sentenced to nearly eight years in jail for kidnapping and manslaughter, amongst other charges. His mother, Xiuyun Li and father, Jingui Liu, had earlier been convicted of kidnapping and misconduct to human remains and are due to be sentenced later this year.

On Tuesday's sentencing, Liu's lawyer asked for leniency arguing that his client feels remorse and "is not a cult leader, nor requires people to follow his cult", according to Radio New Zealand.

New Zealand media outlets reported that Liu had attended a military-based university in China.

In 2011, he was a contestant for China's Got Talent - clips posted online showed him singing onstage blindfolded.

Sometime in 2017, he moved to New Zealand along with Xiao, and the couple became permanent residents.

Liu attracted followers on Chinese social media where he posted religious discussions, video diaries, and clips of himself singing. He also set up a project called Universal Choir that produced cosmic-themed orchestral music.

During the trial a police officer who interviewed one of Liu's female followers gave testimony. He said in court that the woman told him she "met the people over the internet through a song website, and she referred to the occupants of the house as friends".

During the sentencing, Justice Mathew Downs said Liu had shown "callous indifference" towards Wang.

"Because of you, Ms Wang died a lonely, frightening death. You display no remorse whatsoever. You should feel shame."

articles.body: Zoho founder Sridhar Vembu has shared his views on a workplace question many companies face: Should employees wait for instructions from their leaders or take the initiative and act on their own? In a post on X (formerly known as Twitter), Sridhar Vembu said giving people more freedom to take initiative can create an energetic but sometimes chaotic work culture. Employees may disagree strongly with one another and constantly feel that things can be improved. âThere is always the gnawing feeling of ânot good enoughâ,â Vembu wrote, explaining the trade-off between certainty and initiative in an organisation.Sridhar Vembu on why freedom can feel âchaoticâIn the post, Sridhar Vembu said highly metric-driven organisations often create a culture where employees wait for instructions from the top. Such workplaces can offer more predictability and certainty.However, he warned that this approach has its risks. âUnless the top always knows how to set the right course, the org can be lost,â Vembu wrote.On the other hand, an organisation where people are encouraged to take initiative can be less predictable. Employees with energy and strong ideas may disagree with each other, he said.âSeize the initiative cultureâ often feels chaotic, with lots of internal disagreements. There is always the gnawing feeling of ânot good enoughâ,â Vembu wrote.Sridhar Vembu: 'Every smart programmerâ thinks they can do betterThe Zoho founder also used programmers as an example to explain why initiative-driven workplaces can see frequent disagreements.âPeople who are full of energy and initiative often vehemently disagree with other,â he wrote, adding: âI joke about this: every smart programmer looks at another programmer's code and thinks âit sucks, I can do betterâ!âAccording to Vembu, this is the trade-off companies need to understand when building their culture. A workplace can provide employees with comfortable certainty but risk losing their initiative. Alternatively, it can encourage people to take initiative while accepting the discomfort and disagreements that may come with it.Hereâs the post shared by Sridhar Vembu"On org culture: Do people wait for instructions from the top? Or do they seize the initiative and run?Highly metric driven orgs tend to produce the "wait for instructions from the top" culture and there is more predictability and certainty in that culture. Unless the top always knows how to set the right course, the org can be lost."Seize the initiative culture" often feels chaotic, with lots of internal disagreements. There is always the gnawing feeling of "not good enough". In a chaotic initiative-driven culture, the external environment (market) may have to provide the occasional discipline.People who are full of energy and initiative often vehemently disagree with other. I joke about this: every smart programmer looks at another programmer's code and thinks "it sucks, I can do better"!That is your trade-off in org cultures. We can provide comfortable certainty but lose the initiative or we can seize the initiative but keep feeling somewhat uncomfortable.In my experience, trying to square this circle: "we will have a highly disciplined culture of seizing the initiative" produces the worst of both worlds."Get the latest technology news and updates. articles.title: 4 children, 4 adults killed in shooting and fire at Montana home, police say
articles.summary: A motive in the incident in Billings wasn’t immediately provided. Police said they were withholding the identities of the dead for now.
articles.body: Four children and four adults were killed when a gunman opened fire at a Billings, Montana, home that was then set alight, authorities said Tuesday. Billings police released the number but continued to keep identities of the dead undisclosed in what they said is a homicide investigation. “To protect the integrity of this ongoing investigation and the recovery efforts currently underway, no additional information will be released at this time,” the police department said in a joint statement issued with the Yellowstone County Sheriff’s Office. “This a complex process,” they added, citing the structural integrity of the home due to the fire. Police characterized the incident Sunday evening near the city’s West End neighborhood as a family disturbance. The gunman died of a self-inflicted gunshot, NBC affiliate KULR of Billings reported. A possible motive was not available. At a news conference Monday, Interim Yellowstone County Sheriff Kent O’Donnell asked for “patience as we complete this investigation.” Billings police and county sheriff’s deputies were dispatched to the shooting in the 300 block of White Star Circle at 6:01 p.m. Sunday, police said on Facebook. O’Donnell said gunshots could be heard during the 911 call. Officers and deputies reached the scene in roughly 10 minutes and at that point heard gunfire from the back of the residence, the police department said. Three minutes later, the home was fully engulfed in flames, it said. Video from the scene showed law enforcement officers taking cover behind patrol SUVs on the street near the home as a small tactical team behind a handheld shield moved toward the structure. Firefighters were dispatched but may have faced water access issues and fewer fire hydrants than might be ideal, officials said. “The delay in limited access presented significant challenges, fire conditions continued to worsen, and the residents ultimately became ... consumed by fire,” Billings Fire Chief Matt Hoppel said at Monday’s news conference. The origin of the blaze was also under investigation. Billings Police Sgt. Jeff Stovall said in a statement Monday that some information was being withheld “to protect the integrity of the ongoing investigation.” “There are details we simply cannot release at this time,” he said. articles.title: U.S. strikes a vessel in the eastern Pacific, killing 2 people in first attack in months
articles.summary: After a pause of more than two months, the U.S. military announced Monday that it once again carried out a strike on a vessel in the eastern Pacific Ocean, killing two people accused of trafficking drugs.
articles.body: WASHINGTON — After a pause of more than two months, the U.S. military announced Monday that it once again carried out a strike on a vessel in the eastern Pacific Ocean, killing two people accused of trafficking drugs. It brings the overall death toll to 223 people killed in 67 strikes during the nearly yearlong U.S. campaign of bombing alleged drug boats off Latin America’s Caribbean coast and in the eastern Pacific Ocean. U.S. Southern Command says the campaign has resulted in the destruction of 64 speedboats, three “low-profile” ships and a semisubmersible craft. The command said on social media early Monday that forces “executed a lethal kinetic strike on a low-profile vessel operating along established narcotrafficking routes in the Eastern Pacific.” The military said the strike occurred Sunday, and it marked the first since powerful back-to-back June 24 earthquakes in Venezuela killed thousands of people. As with most of the military’s statements, Southern Command did not provide evidence that the vessel was ferrying drugs. “We are committed to imposing total systemic friction on narco-terrorists — disrupting their operations, dismantling their leadership, and eliminating cartel terror across the region,” said Gen. Francis Donovan, who leads U.S. Southern Command. The latest strike comes as the Trump administration pursues deals with allied nations to extend its offensive to land across multiple Latin American countries. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said during a visit to Panama this month that Colombia, Guatemala and Honduras had agreed to allow the U.S. to carry out joint military operations against criminal groups on their soil. Guatemala denied reaching such a deal. Ecuador launched similar missions with the U.S. in March. The Trump administration’s boat-bombing campaign began in early September and has left numerous survivors, but most of them have never been recovered. U.S. Southern Command said in a separate statement Monday that there have been more than 20 search-and-rescue efforts overall, almost all of which were unsuccessful. According to data compiled from the command’s social media posts, the strikes have generated 28 survivors with only three people ever being rescued — one person during a strike in March who was transferred to the Costa Rican Coast Guard, and two wounded people who were later repatriated to their home countries of Ecuador and Colombia. The very first strike in September 2025 left two survivors who were killed in a second, follow-up strike. When that became public, it drew concern from some lawmakers and those who study military law. The White House insisted it was done “in self-defense” to ensure the boat was destroyed and in accordance with armed conflict laws. But some legal scholars said a second strike killing survivors would have been illegal under any circumstance, armed conflict or not. President Donald Trump has said the U.S. is in “armed conflict” with cartels in Latin America and has justified the attacks as a necessary escalation to stem the flow of drugs into the United States and fatal overdoses claiming American lives. But his administration has offered little evidence to support its claims of killing “narcoterrorists.” Critics have questioned the overall legality of the boat strikes as well as their effectiveness, in part because the fentanyl behind many fatal overdoses is typically trafficked to the U.S. over land from Mexico, where it is produced with chemicals imported from China and India. The Pentagon’s watchdog said in May that it plans to look into whether the U.S. military followed an established targeting framework when carrying out the strikes. However, the evaluation is focused specifically on what is known as the six-phase Joint Targeting Cycle and not on the legality of the strikes, the inspector general’s office said.

articles.title: Ladakh protests: Sonam Wangchuk leads Leh candle march, seeks inquiry report into 2025 violence
articles.summary: LEH: Activist Sonam Wangchuk on Monday led a candle march in Leh as part of a month-long programme to remember those who died in the violent clashes i.
articles.body: LEH: Activist Sonam Wangchuk on Monday led a candle march in Leh as part of a month-long programme to remember those who died in the violent clashes in Ladakh last year, while demanding the release of the inquiry commissionâs report into the September 2025 violence this month.Wangchuk said August 24 to September 24 would be observed to commemorate the events of September 24, 2025, when protests over statehood and inclusion of Ladakh in the Sixth Schedule of the Constitution turned violent.A BJP office was set on fire during the unrest and at least four people were killed in police action that followed.Speaking on Monday, Wangchuk said the inquiry commissionâs report should be released this month, arguing that the delay was affecting public confidence. He also said a âdecisive meetingâ between the Leh Apex Body (LAB), Kargil Democratic Alliance (KDA) and the Centre was expected in the first week of September to discuss Ladakhâs demands."This entire month, from August 24 to September 24, is being observed to honour and remember the events of 24 September 2025, which was a dark day. It was a day when five of our young men were martyred, and many others were injured, left disabled, or critically wounded. We began with a small candle march; it was kept small because His Holiness the Dalai Lama is currently in Ladakh. Once he departs, we will commemorate this month with much greater intensity," Wangchuk said.Recalling last yearâs protests, he said Ladakh had been seeking its demands for six years and that a hunger strike began on September 10 after delays in addressing them."Regarding the situation over the past year: Ladakh has been demanding its rights for six years, but faced with delays and reluctance, people began a hunger strike on September 10 to make their voices heard peacefully. By the 15th day, when participants had to be hospitalised in critical condition, the public became deeply distressed and angry; circumstances arose, or were perhaps engineered, that led to some violence, and there is a pressing need for an investigation into this."Wangchuk demanded that the report of the inquiry commission, headed by a retired judge, be made public, ANI reported."We are also calling for action regarding the Inquiry Commission led by a retired judge; a full year has passed, yet no decision has been reached. This delay is eroding public confidence. We hope that the Inquiry Commission's report will be released this month. Regarding the decisions concerning Ladakh's demands, discussed on May 22, no subsequent meeting has taken place to date. We hope that a decisive meeting will take place in the first week of September, as promised; otherwise, we will have to make our voices heard much more loudly, albeit peacefully," Wangchuk said.Wangchuk, who had spearheaded the protests along with the LAB and KDA, was detained for 170 days in Jodhpur Jail following the violence and was released in March 2026.The LAB and KDA have been demanding inclusion of Ladakh in the Sixth Schedule of the Constitution. The Centre, meanwhile, has proposed that the Union Territory administration constitute an Autonomous Hill Development Council in each of Ladakhâs seven districts under a framework based on Article 371.Ladakhâs administrative map expanded from two districts to seven in April, when Sham, Nubra, Changthang, Zanskar and Drass were notified.The next round of talks with the Union Home Ministry is expected in September.(With agency inputs)Stay updated with the latest Srinagar news. articles.title: As elections near, Netanyahu casts Turkey as Israel’s latest enemy
articles.summary: The giant billboard on Tel Aviv’s main highway placed Turkey squarely at the center of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s election campaign. The image showed its president, Recep Tayyip Erdogan, alongside the leaders of Iran, Hezbollah and the mayor of New York City as adversaries of Israel under the slogan, “They want Netanyahu to lose. Don’t let them win.”
articles.body: The giant billboard on Tel Aviv’s main highway placed Turkey squarely at the center of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s election campaign. The image showed its president, Recep Tayyip Erdogan, alongside the leaders of Iran, Hezbollah and the mayor of New York City as adversaries of Israel under the slogan, “They want Netanyahu to lose. Don’t let them win.” Just a few days later, Turkey became the center of Israel’s latest military confrontation as well. Israeli jets struck the Abu al-Dahar airbase in northern Syria, targeting what officials said was an emerging Turkish military buildup that Israel viewed as a significant threat. But with elections just over two months away, the strike’s proximity to Netanyahu’s campaign messaging has fueled a debate in Israel and abroad: is Netanyahu preempting a genuine strategic threat or amplifying one to boost his ballot-box standing? Throughout much of his decades-long political career, Netanyahu has portrayed himself as “Mr. Security,” equipped to confront any threats facing Israel. He is also a shrewd political operator with a long record of turning crises to his advantage. Tom Barrack, US President Donald Trump’s envoy to Syria and ambassador to Turkey, issued a rare public rebuke to Israel over the strike, calling it an “unnecessary escalation.” In an interview with podcaster Mario Nawfal, Barrack suggested a political motive, floating a “theory” that Israel “simply tried to bait Turkey.” He called it “a very aggressive move, but one that might play well going into elections.” Officially, Israel has framed the attack as a pure operational necessity: Netanyahu and his Defense Minister Israel Katz have both said Israeli intelligence indicated Turkey was preparing to install forces and equipment at the airbase. An Israeli military source told CNN the Israel Defense Forces (IDF) had gathered intelligence on Turkey’s plans to deploy personnel, drones and air-defense systems at the site. Such a deployment, the source said, could constrain Israel’s freedom of action in Syrian airspace and alter the strategic balance in the area. The intelligence, a second source said, was shared with the Trump administration and with Syria’s President Ahmed Al-Sharaa. Israel and Syria have held deconfliction talks over the past year, reaching what Netanyahu has described as a “status quo in security matters.” On Sunday, Roman Goffman, the chief of Israel’s Mossad intelligence agency, met again with Syrian Foreign Minister Asaad al-Shaibani in Jordan to ease the latest tensions, according to the Syrian state news agency. Still, Turkey, the US and some of Netanyahu’s domestic political rivals pointed to the timing. Rejecting the Israeli account as “untenable,” Turkey accused Netanyahu of “pursuing expansionist and destabilizing policies in the region” ahead of the October vote. The Turkish government said it would continue to cooperate with the Syrian government “on a legitimate basis for the establishment of peace, stability, and prosperity.” Netanyahu brands Erdogan an ‘antisemitic tyrant’ Netanyahu and Katz have pushed back on the political motivation narrative, warning instead of an impending Turkish footprint in Syria. “We will not tolerate a military Turkish presence taking root in Syria and threatening Israel,” Netanyahu said last week. Meanwhile, the Israeli prime minister also sharpened his already-combative rhetoric against Erdogan. On Friday, Netanyahu’s office branded Erdogan in an X post as an “antisemitic tyrant who oppresses his own people.” Netanyahu and Erdogan have a long-running public feud, which intensified dramatically during the wars in Gaza, Lebanon and Iran. Erdogan has called Netanyahu a war criminal and repeatedly accused Israel of atrocities in Gaza; Netanyahu has accused Erdogan of supporting Hamas. Recently, Netanyahu came out against the sale of US F-35 fighter jets to Ankara, warning of Erdogan’s “aggressive ambitions” in the region. Amos Harel, a senior security analyst for the leftwing Haaretz newspaper, says that both the security and political explanations are relevant. “There are indeed indications that Erdogan’s approach toward Israel is very hostile, and that Turkey is undertaking various military moves in Syria, some of which concern the IDF – including at that specific airport,” he said, citing intelligence on Turkish plans to deploy advisers, drones, and air-defense systems. At the same time, Harel told CNN, “it is also completely clear Netanyahu is pursuing a new and aggressive line,” one he frames as a lesson from the October 7, 2023 attack on Israel: strike first, on every front, while establishing security buffer zones along Israel’s borders in Gaza, Lebanon, and Syria. The Israeli military seized a 400 square kilometer buffer zone inside Syria after the 2024 collapse of the Assad regime and has occupied it since. But the political context of the latest war of words has only deepened the suspicions of some of Netanyahu’s critics. Opposition leader Yair Lapid, who defended the operation itself as justified, criticized the triumphant Israeli statements that followed. “In the Middle East, striking when necessary is important. But if you struck, stay quiet,” he said. Yair Golan, leader of the leftwing Democrats party, called the operation “provocative and dangerous.” Former prime minister Ehud Barak went further, writing on social media that the escalation “strongly reeks of a political intention to go into elections amid a series of security tensions designed to alarm the public.” With Netanyahu and his political bloc currently trailing in the polls, his critics are concerned that a new security crisis could fundamentally shift the political landscape and help him control the campaign agenda. “Netanyahu is known to believe that a security emergency is a last-resort option that could reshuffle the deck and improve his chances of surviving these elections,” Harel said. And with Trump constraining Israel’s war on Iran and limiting its military actions in Gaza and Lebanon, he said, “Turkey-Syria becomes a potential front. This raises, at the very least, a strong suspicion that political considerations are involved as well.”
